title: Solos, leads and applause in the old days
summary: Barnes explains there were no solos as such, only special parts or leads to rest other horns' lips, and audiences clapped at the end of a number, not for solos.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Did they take solos where they would be the only horn playing? Did they do any of that, Mealy?

Well, I'mma tell you about that right now, horn. For us solos, I never heard solos in my life until, uh, as late to him. Because the only solos that we have when we play all, uh, two that had clarinet parts in it. That was the only solo. Oh, I see. Special parts like, uh. Yeah. Special, that's direct for them clarinet or chime on or call that, you see. But if this would take a solo, we didn't do that. Only solo that we would take, well, we wouldn't call it solo. We'd call it a, uh, a lead. That's in order for a chime on or a trumpet or all the rest to dry their lips.
Then we'd call it another part and they'd come in and allow for it. I see. So, you wouldn't necessarily, uh, take the lead in the same place in the same tune every time you played it.

No, sir. I never known of that. That's just right to him. And it would just come up. Yeah. I never heard of that before, but, uh, that, that's really a new style, which I believe, I'm sure, that any old musician will tell you that.
Well, now you mentioned some tunes where they have special clarinet parts. What would some of the tunes be like that?

Well, I can't pretty much remember the tune now, but such as Grace and Brody and Grace and Beauty and, uh, and, uh, Black and White, and, uh, well, it's different numbers. So I can't remember this part of his list now. You see, well, uh, you see it says it's Panama. Well, a Panama was a number that would play pretty much a good tempo number for a phone number. But, uh, uh, uh, in that, for a man to take a solo, it had to be to dry your lips.

It had to be his dry lips. Like when you play, we both playing together, well, he'd say hold it for a while. You see, all you say hold it. Well, you hold it, you sit on it, take a rest day, you move on. By the time I come back in, that's the way I'll figure it out. But for instance, a solo now, I don't know, it's different. Uh-huh. Yeah, pretty much all of them in the ground is different. It's hard to get a, uh, a real Dixieland man who's out there for us to find out, you catch some of the first men, such as, uh, Peter Bugga, or, well, that's about the only man here that I can remember just now leading. But anyhow, some of the old-time men, real old-time men are the second-class men as myself. Yeah. Cause see, Peter, I put them before me. Yeah. And I'm second one, the rest is off.
Uh-huh. Yeah. Well, now, I mean, back in the old days when you would play, take the lead, would the people applaud after you finished taking the clarinet part alone like you do now?
Yeah, they'd applaud for individual things like that.

Uh-huh. Well, they applaud for it at that time, but at the meantime, when the tune was empty, when the tune was through, they'd stop and they'd stop and they'd clap and clap and tell you, you had to play it over, they wouldn't stop. But for us to have taken a solo and they'd clap? No. No.
No. But at the end of the number?

At the end of the number, if a person like the tune of a bunch on the floor would like that to- They'd like to hold to them. They'd stand up and they'd clap, they'd stomp, they'd holler, they'd do everything, to get that number going over again. After it gets going over, well, it's all right, they'd be satisfied.
Now this is a really long time when I'm giving it up and all that nobody will tell you anything.
